newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa grants amnesty to three apartheid hit-men.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa grants amnesty to three apartheid hit-men.

text.p: A former South African police hit squad leader was on Monday granted amnesty from prosecution for the murder of an anti-apartheid lawyer, eight years after lifting the lid on state-ordered assassinations.

Dirk Coetzee and two black accomplices, David Tshikalanga and Almond Nofomela, were granted amnesty by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission for the fatal stabbing of lawyer Griffiths Mxenge in November 1981.
A lawyer for Mxenge's family, which has opposed the application from the start, said on state radio on Monday night he would challenge the decision in the High Court.
"We'll be asking the court to set aside this decision of the committee on amnesty and declare it null, void and of no force and effect," lawyer Imraan Moosa said.
"We will ask the court to refer the matter to an independent and impartial committee on amnesty to be set up," Moosa added, without elaborating.
The truth commission's amnesty panel said in a statement the three men's request was granted on the grounds that they had acted on the orders of senior police officers.

"We are satisfied that they did what they did because they regarded it as their duty as policemen who were engaged in the struggle against the African National Congress (ANC) and other liberation movements," the panel added.

The trio were convicted of the murder in May this year by the High Court in the Indian Ocean port city of Durban where Mxenge had lived. The trial was suspended pending the outcome of the amnesty hearing, and they will now not be sentenced.

Mxenge acted for anti-apartheid activists charged with political offences. Coetzee said in his testimony that Mxenge became "a thorn in the flesh" of the security police for his success in gaining detainees the protection of the courts.

A former police captain, Coetzee defected to the ANC after blowing the whistle in 1989 on the clandestine "Vlakplaas" police unit he headed as well as a series of murders carried out by the unit's covert hit squads in the fight against the ANC.
Nofomela and Tshikalange both worked for Vlakplaas, situated on a farm west of Pretoria.
Coetzee, who was the target of a failed assassination attempt by his former colleagues after he defected, now works for President Nelson Mandela's espionage service.
The truth commission's amnesty panel said all three had also requested amnesty for a host of other human rights violations.
Apart from confirming these would be dealt with separately, the panel did not indicate when a final adjudication of their cases could be expected.
Coetzee has asked for amnesty for 23 incidents, of which 14 are crimes or acts involving gross human rights abuses. Tshikalange is seeking amnesty for seven and Nofomela 22 cases.

The truth commission, tasked with uncovering apartheid-era abuses, has sought to persuade offenders to come clean in return for amnesty from criminal prosecution and private litigation. Coetzee's application was seen by many observers as a test case.
